analysis.one_liner: Writes the 2018 rule allowing three years of ACA-exempt short-term health insurance into law.
analysis.headline: The bill never went anywhere: it had zero cosponsors and sat in the Senate Health Committee until the Congress ended in January 2021, with no hearing and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would lock into federal law a 2018 rule that lets insurers sell "short-term, limited-duration" health plans for up to 12 months at a time, renewable out to three years total. These plans are exempt from the Affordable Care Act's rules, so they can turn people down or charge more for preexisting conditions, skip benefits like maternity care and prescription drugs, and impose dollar caps. The bill would also create a new "renewal guarantee" that lets insurers charge an extra fee for the right to re-buy coverage later at a locked price.
analysis.who_benefits: Insurers that sell short-term, ACA-exempt plans gain a permanent statutory market: coverage lasting up to three years, plus a new product — the paid "renewal guarantee" — that collects extra premiums up front. Healthy, uninsured people who can pass medical underwriting also gain, because these plans are cheaper than ACA-compliant coverage.

how_it_helps.text: Codifies the 2018 rule that raised the maximum length of short-term, limited-duration plans from under 3 months to under 12 months initially, renewable to 36 months total, instead of leaving the expansion to future regulators.

Creates a statutory 'renewal guarantee' letting insurers charge an extra amount at initial enrollment in exchange for the option to buy a later policy at a locked premium with no new medical underwriting — a new revenue product for these insurers.

Gives healthy uninsured people a cheaper coverage option by exempting these plans from ACA market rules, while requiring only a 14-point-type notice warning buyers that the plan can exclude preexisting conditions, maternity care, prescription drugs, mental health care, and impose lifetime or annual dollar limits.

analysis.who_pays: People with preexisting conditions pay twice: they generally cannot use these plans, and as healthier people leave ACA-compliant markets for cheaper short-term coverage, premiums in those markets rise for those who remain. Short-term plan buyers also bear real risk — the bill's own required notice says they can face coverage gaps and may have to wait for an open enrollment period to get other insurance if the coverage expires.
analysis.who_pays_short: People with preexisting conditions and ACA enrollees

drawbacks.text: The plans are expressly exempt from the ACA's market rules: they can deny or price coverage based on health history, omit essential benefits like hospitalization, emergency services, maternity care, and mental health treatment, and impose lifetime or annual dollar limits — leaving buyers with coverage that can fail exactly when they get sick.

When a short-term plan expires or the buyer loses eligibility, the buyer may have to wait until an open enrollment period to obtain other coverage — a gap in protection the bill's own required warning notice describes.

By pulling healthier people out of ACA-compliant insurance pools, the expansion raises premiums for the people left behind, particularly those with preexisting conditions, who are the very people the ACA rules were designed to protect.
The bill would make the 2018 expansion permanent statute, so a future administration could not tighten the rules through regulation without another act of Congress.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: healthy uninsured people get cheaper premiums. The costs fall broadly — buyers hold coverage that can exclude the care they eventually need, and sicker people face higher premiums as risk pools thin. Making the 2018 rule permanent statute, rather than reversible regulation, is the main prize for insurers; for consumers, the trade is a lower price for much weaker coverage, and the bill's own warning notice concedes the risk.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, got no cosponsors, and died there when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Kelly Loeffler introduced the bill on May 21, 2020, during the first months of the COVID-19 pandemic.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which took no further action on it.
No senator from either party signed on as a cosponsor, no hearing or markup was held, and the bill never reached the Senate floor before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained much, because nothing happened. The ACA's existing consumer protections — including the limits that kept short-term plans to shorter durations — simply stayed in place, while insurers hoping for a permanent statutory market for three-year ACA-exempt plans got nothing.

for.name: Sen. Kelly Loeffler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 21, 2020, to give statutory force to the 2018 short-term plan rule; recruited no cosponsors.

for.name: Treasury, Labor, and HHS Departments
for.role: Agencies that issued the 2018 short-term insurance rule
for.what_they_did: Issued the October 2018 rule that the bill would write permanently into law.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the referral on May 21, 2020 — no hearing, no markup, no vote — letting the bill die when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever held and the sole sponsor was a Republican with zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.note: The bill converts a temporary regulatory rule into permanent law, guaranteeing these insurers a three-year market for plans exempt from ACA rules and adding a paid 'renewal guarantee' product. They profit by insuring the healthy, which leaves sicker people in ACA plans bearing higher premiums.

Letting healthier people buy ACA-exempt plans for up to three years thins out ACA-compliant risk pools, raising average claims costs for the insurers that must accept all comers. Their interest in the bill runs alongside the public's, since keeping healthier enrollees in also holds down premiums for sick ones.
